0.points.1.label: The Climatic Watershed

1.title: A Shared Geological Origin, Different Climatic Fates
1.html:
Alsace and the German Rhine / Mosel regions both sit on a fractured geological belt born in the formation of the Rhine Rift Valley millions of years ago — which is why the soils of both show extremely high diversity. But their climatic fates are very different:

  • Alsace (Colmar): the Vosges block rain clouds from the west, with annual rainfall of about 500–600 mm, and it is often called the second-driest town in all France (after Perpignan in the south); about 1,800 hours of sunshine a year, an annual mean temperature of 10–11°C, and a growing-season (April–September) mean above 16°C
  • German Mosel / Rheingau: a continental climate with moderate rainfall and a long autumn — especially important for late-ripening varieties such as Riesling, and the climatic basis for ultra-sweet wines such as BA, TBA and Eiswein

💡 Alsace's dry, low-rainfall climate lets grapes reach full ripeness more easily; Germany's long, cool autumn lets grapes slowly accumulate sugar and aroma on the vine while keeping high acidity.
2.title: Soils and Terrain Compared
2.items.0.label: Alsace
2.items.0.desc: Gentle slopes at the foot of the Vosges, with extremely diverse soil types (granite, limestone, marl, volcanic rock, sandstone and more), with varieties planted to match the geological zones
2.items.1.label: Mosel-Saar-Ruwer
2.items.1.desc: Steep slate slopes, where slate stores heat and reflects sunlight, giving Riesling its signature flint / mineral character
3.title: The Fundamental Difference in Classification Logic
3.html:
The classification systems of the two regions reflect very different philosophies of quality:

  • Alsace (the French system): centred on fixed appellation tiers — AOC Alsace → 51 legally defined Grand Cru sites → VT / SGN (by minimum natural sugar at harvest, in g/L, with chaptalisation forbidden)
  • The German system: centred on the ripeness sugar of the fruit at harvest (Oechsle degrees), regardless of the site tier — QmP from low to high runs Kabinett → Spätlese → Auslese → Beerenauslese (BA) → Eiswein → Trockenbeerenauslese (TBA); Germany also has the VDP (Die Prädikatsweingüter), an estate-association classification independent of the official one, ranking vineyard quality into Erste Lage / Grosse Lage tiers

In short: Alsace first asks "which plot is this?", while Germany first asks "how ripe were the grapes at harvest?" — which is also the most important difference in mindset when tasting in the two regions.
4.title: Style Compared: Riesling as the Example
4.html:
FeatureAlsace RieslingGerman Riesling (Mosel / Rheingau)
Sweetness tendencyThe great majority are dry (sec)From very dry (trocken) to very sweet (TBA / Eiswein), a wide spectrum
AlcoholUsually higher (12.5–13.5%)Usually lower (7.5–11%), especially in sweet styles
BodyMedium to full, with rich, direct fruitLight and delicate, with prominent minerality
Dominant aromasLime, honey, slate (ripe fruit dominant)Green apple, white flowers, flinty minerality, with petrol notes emerging with age
5.question: What is the most fundamental difference in logic between the Alsace and German wine classification systems?
5.options.0: Alsace has no classification system at all
5.options.1: Alsace is centred on fixed appellation tiers (AOC → Grand Cru → VT/SGN); Germany is centred on the ripeness sugar of the fruit at harvest (Oechsle degrees), regardless of the site tier
5.options.2: The classification logic of the two is exactly the same
5.options.3: Germany has only one classification: QbA
5.explanation: Alsace first asks "which plot is this?" — centred on fixed appellation and Grand Cru tiers; Germany first asks "how ripe were the grapes at harvest?" — Oechsle degrees decide the tier from Kabinett to TBA, regardless of vineyard location (the VDP is a separate estate-association classification independent of the official one).
6.message: Alsace vs Germany comparative tasting complete!
6.keyPoints.0: The two regions share the geological origin of the Rhine rift but have different climatic fates: Alsace is dry and low in rainfall (the Vosges rain shadow), Germany has a continental climate with a long autumn
6.keyPoints.1: Soils and terrain: Alsace's gentle slopes of diverse geology vs the Mosel's steep slate slopes
6.keyPoints.2: Classification logic: Alsace looks at appellation tier (AOC → Grand Cru → VT/SGN); Germany looks at sugar at harvest (Kabinett → TBA)
6.keyPoints.3: Riesling style compared: Alsace mostly dry, higher in alcohol, rich in fruit; Germany with a wide spectrum, lower in alcohol, prominent minerality
